sedetani.t: An Iberian people of the middle Ebro around Salduie, the native town on whose site Augustus founded Caesaraugusta, modern Zaragoza.
sedetani.o: The Sedetani occupied the middle Ebro valley around modern Zaragoza from at least the 5th century BCE. They belonged to the Iberian world, with fortified towns on hills and terraces above the river and its tributaries.
sedetani.r: Their main centre was Salduie, which minted coins with the Iberian legend Salduie. Farming of the fertile Ebro plain, livestock and trade along the river underpinned their economy. They are sometimes confused in ancient texts with the Edetani of Valencia. Horsemen from Salduie served Rome in the Social War and received citizenship in 89 BCE, recorded on the Bronze of Ascoli.
sedetani.e: The Sedetani were brought under Roman control during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and became part of Hispania Citerior. Around 14 BCE Augustus founded the colony of Caesaraugusta on the site of Salduie, and the Sedetani merged into Roman provincial society.

selinous.t: The westernmost Greek city in Sicily, famed for its great temples, which was destroyed by Carthage in 409 BCE.
selinous.o: Colonists from Megara Hyblaea, led by Pammilus, founded Selinous around 628 BCE on a coastal plateau between two rivers in south-western Sicily, according to Thucydides; some ancient sources give an earlier date. The name came from wild celery (selinon), which appears on its coins.
selinous.r: Selinous grew rich from its grain-growing lands and trade with Carthage and the Elymians, and it built more large temples than almost any other Greek city: on its acropolis and on the eastern hill stand the remains of at least eight, including the colossal Temple G, and their sculpted metopes are now in Palermo. It sided with Carthage in 480 BCE but later quarrelled over borders with Segesta, which called in Athens and Carthage.
selinous.e: In 409 BCE a Carthaginian army under Hannibal Mago stormed Selinous after nine days, killing thousands. The city revived under Carthaginian control, but in 250 BCE Carthage moved its inhabitants to Lilybaeum and abandoned it. Its archaeological park is one of the largest in Europe.

sasanian-yemen.t: Yemen as a province of the Persian Empire, ruled by a Persian garrison whose descendants, the Abna, helped bring the country into Islam.
sasanian-yemen.o: Around 570 the Sasanian king Khosrow I sent a small force under the general Wahriz at the request of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan to expel the Ethiopians of Aksumite Yemen. Sayf was set up as a client ruler, but after his murder Persia took direct control, governing from Sanaa through a marzban.
sasanian-yemen.r: Persian rule was light and focused on Sanaa and the trade routes. Persian soldiers settled and married locally, forming the Abna, a distinct elite group. Yemen gave the Sasanian Empire a foothold on the Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade against the Byzantine Empire and its allies, but the provincial governors had limited reach into the tribal highlands.
sasanian-yemen.e: As Persia weakened after its wars with Byzantium, the governor Badhan accepted Islam around 628 and Yemen came under the Islamic state of Medina. The Abna remained influential in early Islamic Sanaa.

sequani.t: Gallic people of Franche-Comté whose rivalry with the Aedui led them to invite the German Ariovistus into Gaul.
sequani.o: The Sequani lived between the Saône, the Jura and the Rhine, around their great oppidum of Vesontio (Besançon) in a loop of the Doubs. Their land was famous for salted pork exported to Rome.
sequani.r: They contested with the Aedui for control of tolls on the Saône and for leadership of Gaul. Caesar names Catamantaloedes as a former king who held the title of friend of the Roman people, and his son Casticus as a would-be king.
sequani.e: To defeat the Aedui they hired the German leader Ariovistus, who then seized a third of their land, until Caesar drove him out in 58 BCE. The Sequani joined the revolt of 52 BCE. Under Rome Vesontio became an important town, and their land later formed the province of Maxima Sequanorum.

second-taifa-of-cordoba.t: Córdoba's brief independence under the qadi Ibn Hamdin during the collapse of Almoravid rule in al-Andalus in the 1140s.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.o: In 1144, amid revolts across al-Andalus against the Almoravids, the Córdoban qadi Ibn Hamdin, from a leading family of jurists, was proclaimed emir by the city's notables and expelled the Almoravid garrison.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.r: Ibn Hamdin's authority rested on his religious office and local support rather than on an army. He briefly claimed recognition from other cities, but was driven out for a time by the Hudid prince Zafadola and had to seek help from Alfonso VII of Castile, while the Almoravid commander Yahya ibn Ghaniya fought to retake the city.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.e: Ibn Hamdin fled to North Africa, and by 1148 Córdoba had passed to the Almohads, who made Seville their main Andalusi capital. Córdoba fell to Ferdinand III of the Crown of Castile in 1236.

sarmatians.t: Iranian-speaking horse nomads who replaced the Scythians as masters of the Pontic steppe and fought Rome for four centuries.
sarmatians.o: The Sarmatians grew out of the Sauromatae, whom Herodotus placed east of the Don. From the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE their tribes pushed west across the Don and Dnieper, breaking the power of the Scythians and taking over the steppe as far as the Danube. Leading tribes included the Iazyges, Roxolani, Aorsi, Siraces and later the Alans.
sarmatians.r: They formed a loose confederation of tribes under their own kings rather than a single state. Their armoured lancers on horseback impressed Greek and Roman writers, and rich female burials with weapons suggest women held unusual status, feeding Greek tales of the Amazons. They traded with the Bosporan cities and took Roman subsidies or raided the frontier in turn.
sarmatians.e: Many Sarmatians were absorbed by the Goths in the 3rd century, and the Hunnic invasion of the 370s scattered the rest. Some joined the Huns, others entered Roman service, including 5,500 Iazyges sent to Britain in 175, while the Alans migrated as far as Gaul, Spain and North Africa.

second-bulgarian-empire.t: Restored medieval Bulgarian state of the Asen dynasty, centred on Tarnovo, which defeated the Latin crusaders and led Orthodox culture until the Ottomans came.
second-bulgarian-empire.o: In 1185 the brothers Asen and Peter led a revolt against Byzantine taxes at Tarnovo, restoring Bulgarian independence lost when the First Bulgarian Empire fell in 1018. Their younger brother Kaloyan received a crown from Pope Innocent III in 1204 and in 1205 destroyed the Latin crusader army at Adrianople, capturing Emperor Baldwin I.
second-bulgarian-empire.r: The tsar ruled from the fortified hill of Tsarevets with a council of boyars. Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) defeated Epirus at Klokotnitsa in 1230 and ruled from the Adriatic to the Black Sea, and the Bulgarian patriarchate was restored in 1235. Mongol raids and civil wars weakened the state after 1242. Under Ivan Alexander in the 14th century, Tarnovo became a centre of art and letters, with Patriarch Euthymius reforming church books.
second-bulgarian-empire.e: In 1356 the realm split, with the Tsardom of Vidin breaking away. The Ottomans took Tarnovo in 1393 and Vidin in 1396, and Bulgaria remained under Ottoman rule until 1878.

sexenio-democratico.t: Six turbulent years of revolution in Spain, from the fall of Isabella II through an elected king and a republic to the return of the Bourbons.
sexenio-democratico.o: In September 1868 a military rising led by Generals Juan Prim and Francisco Serrano and Admiral Juan Bautista Topete, known as the Glorious Revolution, drove Isabella II into exile. A provisional government called elections by universal male suffrage, and the Constitution of 1869 declared Spain a constitutional monarchy.
sexenio-democratico.r: With the throne vacant, Serrano acted as regent while Prim searched Europe for a king, a search that helped trigger the Franco-Prussian War. The Cortes chose Amadeo of Savoy, but Prim was assassinated in December 1870, days before he arrived. Amadeo faced Carlist rebellion, war in Cuba and fractious parties, and abdicated in February 1873.
sexenio-democratico.e: The Spanish First Republic followed, collapsing into the Pavía coup of January 1874. In December 1874 General Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII at Sagunto, opening Restoration Spain.

second-taifa-of-almeria.t: Almería's brief independence in the 1140s, ended when a Castilian, Genoese and Catalan crusade stormed the great port in 1147.
second-taifa-of-almeria.o: In 1145 the people of Almería, then the chief Andalusi port and naval base, rose against the Almoravids. Power passed to local leaders, notably the admiral Ibn Maymun, whose family had commanded the Almoravid fleet.
second-taifa-of-almeria.r: Almería remained a centre of silk weaving and Mediterranean trade, but also of corsair raiding against Christian shipping, which made it a target for Genoa and Pisa. Its new rulers had little time to establish a stable government.
second-taifa-of-almeria.e: In October 1147 Alfonso VII of Castile, with Genoese, Pisan, Catalan and Navarrese forces, captured Almería after a siege, creating Castilian Almería.

souliote-confederacy.t: Self-governing community of Orthodox warrior clans in the mountains of Epirus, famous for resisting Ali Pasha of Ioannina for over a decade.
souliote-confederacy.o: Souli was a group of villages in the rugged mountains of Thesprotia in Epirus. From the mid-17th century Orthodox Christian families, mainly Albanian-speaking, settled there and built a free community outside effective Ottoman control, growing into a confederation of villages such as Souli, Kiafa, Avariko and Samoniva.
souliote-confederacy.r: Souliote society was organised in clans (fares), each with its own leader; a council of chiefs decided on war. Men were full-time warriors who lived from herding and from tribute imposed on surrounding villages; women also fought. Leading families included the Botsaris and Tzavelas. The Souliotes spoke Albanian and Greek and were Orthodox.
souliote-confederacy.e: Ali Pasha of Ioannina attacked repeatedly from 1792 and finally forced their surrender in December 1803. Many Souliotes went to Corfu, while women reportedly threw themselves from the cliffs at Zalongo. They returned to fight in the Greek War of Independence under Markos Botsaris.

silures.t: Warlike people of south-east Wales who resisted Rome for nearly thirty years, until legions at Caerleon held their land and Caerwent became their town.
silures.o: The Silures lived in the valleys and coastal plain of Glamorgan and Gwent, defended by hillforts such as Llanmelin. Tacitus, noting their dark complexions and curly hair, speculated that they had come from Spain, a guess no longer accepted. They first appear in 47, when Rome began its advance into Wales.
silures.r: Little is known of their leadership; they seem to have been a confederation of communities rather than a single kingdom, without a coinage of their own. Their warfare relied on raids and ambush in difficult country. Caratacus fought alongside them after 47, and in 52 they defeated a legion under Manlius Valens; the governor Ostorius Scapula died worn out by the campaign.
silures.e: Julius Frontinus finally subdued them around 74 to 78 and founded the legionary fortress of Isca at Caerleon. Their territory became a civitas within Roman Britain with its centre at Venta Silurum, Caerwent, where an inscription records the council of the Silures. The later Kingdom of Gwent grew in the same region.

state-of-brazil.t: The Portuguese royal government of Brazil set up at Salvador in 1549, which united the captaincies under a governor-general and later a viceroy.
state-of-brazil.o: The hereditary captaincies of 1534 had largely failed, so King John III created a central government in 1549. Tomé de Sousa arrived as the first governor-general with soldiers, officials and the first Jesuits under Manuel da Nóbrega, and founded Salvador on the Bay of All Saints as capital.
state-of-brazil.r: The governor-general oversaw defence, justice and finance, while the captaincies kept their own governors. Mem de Sá expelled the French from France Antarctique and founded Rio de Janeiro. In 1621 the north was separated as the State of Maranhão, reporting directly to Lisbon. From the 1640s governors often held the title of viceroy. A High Court, the Relação, sat at Salvador from 1609. The capital moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1763.
state-of-brazil.e: After the Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1808, the colonial government was overshadowed by the monarchy itself. In 1815 the State of Brazil was raised to the Kingdom of Brazil.

second-taifa-of-murcia.t: The kingdom of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King, who ruled eastern al-Andalus for 25 years in alliance with Christian powers against the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-murcia.o: Muhammad ibn Mardanish, of a family of Muwallad origin from the Valencia region, took power in Murcia in 1147 amid the collapse of the Almoravids, soon adding Valencia, Jaén, Dénia and other eastern towns to his domains.
second-taifa-of-murcia.r: Known to Christians as Rey Lobo, he made treaties with Castile, Barcelona, Genoa and Pisa, hired Christian mercenaries and minted gold coins widely used in Christian Iberia. He built palaces such as the Castillejo de Monteagudo near Murcia and kept a sophisticated court while fighting the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-murcia.e: After losing allies and territory, Ibn Mardanish died in 1172, and his sons submitted to the Almohads, who married into his family. Murcia later revived as the Third Taifa of Murcia.

salian-franks.t: Frankish group settled in Toxandria by Rome in 358, whose kings at Tournai founded the Merovingian dynasty.
salian-franks.o: The Salians were one of the Frankish peoples living near the lower Rhine. In 358 the Caesar Julian defeated them but allowed them to settle in Toxandria, in the modern Kempen, as allies of the Roman Empire. Over the next century they moved south-west towards the Scheldt.
salian-franks.r: Their kings served Rome as federate commanders. Around the 440s King Chlodio took Cambrai and the land up to the Somme. The Lex Salica, written down under Clovis, preserves their customary law, including the rule later used to bar women from the French throne.
salian-franks.e: Childeric I, son of Merovech, ruled from Tournai and fought for Rome on the Loire; his rich tomb, found in 1653, held a signet ring and gold bees. On his death in 481 his son Clovis began the conquests that created the Kingdom of the Franks.

serbia.t: Present-day Serbia, independent successor of the Yugoslav states since 2006, an EU candidate that does not recognise Kosovo's independence.
serbia.o: When Montenegro voted to leave Serbia and Montenegro in 2006, Serbia became the legal successor of the union and of the earlier Yugoslav states on 5 June 2006. A new constitution adopted in October 2006 described Kosovo, then under United Nations administration, as an integral part of Serbia.
serbia.r: Serbia is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia rejects, though the EU-brokered Brussels Agreement of 2013 began a normalisation of relations. Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party has dominated politics since 2012, combining EU accession talks with close ties to Russia and China. Manufacturing, agriculture and IT drive the economy.
serbia.e: Serbia became an EU candidate in 2012 and opened accession negotiations in 2014. The collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed sixteen people, led to the largest student-led protests in decades against corruption and Vučić's government.

santones.t: Gallic people of Saintonge on the Atlantic coast, whose land was the goal of the Helvetian migration of 58 BCE.
santones.o: The Santones lived north of the Gironde estuary, along the Charente, in the modern Charente-Maritime. Caesar records that the Helvetii planned to settle in their land, which alarmed him because it lay close to the Roman Province.
santones.r: Their coast gave them ships and seamen, which Caesar requisitioned in 56 BCE for the war against the Veneti. They struck coins in large numbers and traded salt and goods along the Atlantic.
santones.e: They joined the revolt of 52 BCE with twelve thousand men. Under Rome Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) became the first capital of Aquitania, with the Arch of Germanicus and a large amphitheatre. The region kept their name as Saintonge.

sotiates.t: Aquitanian people of the Sos district whose king Adiatuanus made a last stand against Rome with six hundred sworn companions.
sotiates.o: The Sotiates were one of the Aquitani, living around the oppidum of Sos in the modern Lot-et-Garonne, north of the Pyrenean foothills. They are known almost entirely from Caesar's account of the campaign of his legate Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
sotiates.r: Caesar describes their king Adiatuanus surrounded by six hundred soldurii, sworn companions who vowed to share their lord's fate and never survive him. Coins inscribed with the names of the Sotiates and of Adiatuanus confirm the account.
sotiates.e: Crassus defeated the Sotiates in open battle and besieged their oppidum, defeating Roman siege works with mines dug by men skilled in copper mining. After a failed sortie Adiatuanus surrendered. Their land later formed part of the Roman province of Aquitania.

swedish-pomerania.t: Baltic territory held by the Swedish crown for nearly two centuries, giving Sweden a foothold and a vote in the Holy Roman Empire.
swedish-pomerania.o: Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania in 1630 and occupied the duchy during the Thirty Years' War. When the last Pomeranian duke died in 1637, Sweden kept control, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 granted it Western Pomerania with Stettin, Stralsund and the island of Rügen, held as an imperial fief.
swedish-pomerania.r: The Swedish king sat in the Imperial Diet as Duke of Pomerania, but the territory kept its own estates and German law. Greifswald University continued as a centre of learning. Sweden lost Stettin and the lands south of the Peene to Prussia in 1720, and Stralsund became the seat of government. Serfdom was abolished in 1806 under Gustav IV Adolf.
swedish-pomerania.e: Under the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 Sweden ceded Pomerania to Denmark, which exchanged it with Prussia in 1815 for Saxe-Lauenburg and money. It became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania; Swedish influence survives in Stralsund's architecture.

suessiones.t: Belgic people of the Aisne valley whose kings once ruled across Gaul and Britain, and who led the coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE.
suessiones.o: The Suessiones held fertile land along the Aisne, around Soissons. Caesar was told that within living memory their king Diviciacus had been the most powerful ruler in Gaul, holding sway over much of Belgic Gaul and over Britain.
suessiones.r: They shared laws and magistrates with their neighbours the Remi, and Caesar credits them with twelve fortified towns and fifty thousand warriors. Their king Galba was chosen to command the Belgic league in 57 BCE.
suessiones.e: After the league dispersed, Caesar besieged their oppidum of Noviodunum, and the Suessiones surrendered and were placed under the Remi. Under Rome their town Augusta Suessionum became Soissons, later capital of the Domain of Soissons and of Frankish kingdoms.

sogn.t: Petty kingdom around the Sognefjord, Norway's longest fjord, absorbed into Harald Fairhair's realm in the late 9th century.
sogn.o: Sogn, the land around the great Sognefjord in western Norway, appears in the sagas as one of the small kingdoms of the Viking Age. Rich graves along the fjord show a prosperous elite in the Iron Age, but its rulers are known only from late Icelandic tradition.
sogn.r: Its people farmed the fjord slopes, raised livestock in mountain pastures and traded along the coast and over the mountains to eastern Norway. The site of the Gulating, the great law assembly of western Norway, lay at Gulen near the mouth of the fjord, and the district later belonged to its law province.
sogn.e: The sagas say Harald Fairhair took Sogn during his conquest of the west coast and placed it under one of his earls. It became part of the Kingdom of Norway; in the Middle Ages Sogn was known for its stave churches, including Urnes, now a World Heritage Site.

syrian-arab-republic.t: The Syrian state since 1961, ruled for over five decades by the Ba'ath party and the Assad family, and transformed by civil war.
syrian-arab-republic.o: After Syrian officers broke away from the United Arab Republic in September 1961, the country took the name Syrian Arab Republic. A coup on 8 March 1963 brought the Ba'ath party to power, and a further coup in 1966 brought its radical wing.
syrian-arab-republic.r: Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970 and built a one-party state dominated by the army and security services, drawing heavily on his Alawite community. Syria lost the Golan Heights to Israel in 1967, intervened in Lebanon from 1976 and crushed an Islamist uprising at Hama in 1982. Bashar al-Assad succeeded his father in 2000. Repression of protests in 2011 led to a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced half the population.
syrian-arab-republic.e: On 8 December 2024 a rebel offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus and Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia. Ahmed al-Sharaa became interim president in 2025, leading a transitional government.

seven-slavic-tribes.t: Union of Slavic tribes in Moesia that joined Asparuh's Bulgars in 681, forming one of the two founding peoples of Bulgaria.
seven-slavic-tribes.o: After the collapse of the Danube frontier in the early 7th century, Slavs settled densely in Moesia between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains. Byzantine chroniclers, chiefly Theophanes, say seven tribes there formed a union, though their names are not recorded.
seven-slavic-tribes.r: Little is known beyond a few lines in Byzantine chronicles. The union was a loose alliance of farming tribes under their own chiefs, probably formed against Avar and Byzantine pressure. When Asparuh's Bulgars crossed the Danube, the Slavs were placed to guard the western frontier against the Avars, while the Severi held the eastern passes.
seven-slavic-tribes.e: In 681 Byzantium recognised the new Bulgar state, and the union was absorbed into the First Bulgarian Empire. Over the next two centuries Slavs and Bulgars merged, and the Slavic language prevailed.

sahib-ataids.t: A beylik around Afyonkarahisar founded by the family of Sahib Ata, the great Seljuk vizier and builder of Konya.
sahib-ataids.o: Sahib Ata Fakhr al-Din Ali was vizier of the Sultanate of Rum for decades under Mongol overlordship. In the 1270s his sons were granted Karahisar, Kutahya and nearby lands, which the family held as a semi-independent domain after Seljuk authority collapsed.
sahib-ataids.r: Sahib Ata was one of the greatest patrons of Seljuk architecture, building the Ince Minareli madrasa and his own mosque complex in Konya and works in Kayseri and Sivas. His descendants ruled a small beylik in western Anatolia, built mosques and schools in Afyonkarahisar and kept close ties with the Mevlevi order.
sahib-ataids.e: The beylik was squeezed by the Germiyanids, who absorbed its lands by around 1341.

suebi.t: A broad grouping of Germanic peoples between the Elbe and the Rhine whose name Roman writers used for half of Germania and which later gave Swabia its name.
suebi.o: The Suebi enter history in 58 BCE when Julius Caesar fought their leader Ariovistus in Alsace, after he had crossed the Rhine about 72 BCE to aid the Sequani. Caesar describes the Suebi as the largest and most warlike people of Germania. Tacitus later used the name for a whole cluster of peoples around the Elbe, including the Semnones, Marcomanni and Quadi.
suebi.r: The Suebi were less a single state than a loose family of tribes sharing cult and customs. Tacitus describes the 'Suebian knot' hairstyle worn by free warriors and an annual sacrifice in the sacred grove of the Semnones, regarded as the oldest and noblest of the group. Leadership rested with kings or war-leaders chosen for campaigns, and their economy combined farming with cattle raising.
suebi.e: After the 3rd century the name was absorbed into new groupings, especially the Alemanni, whose land became known as Swabia. A separate Suebian group crossed the Rhine in 406 and founded a kingdom in Gallaecia in north-west Spain, which lasted until the Visigoths conquered it in 585.

salyes.t: Celto-Ligurian confederation inland of Marseille whose wars with Greek Massalia drew Rome into Gaul and led to the founding of Aix-en-Provence.
salyes.o: The Salyes were a league of Ligurian and Celtic communities in lower Provence, between the Rhône and the Var. Greek writers mention them from the 4th century BCE as troublesome neighbours of Massalia. Their chief stronghold was the oppidum of Entremont on a plateau north of modern Aix, fortified in the 2nd century BCE.
salyes.r: Entremont is known for its stone sculptures of seated warriors and carved severed heads, and for a portico where real skulls were displayed, reflecting a warrior cult of the head. The Salyes farmed olives and cereals, pressed oil and traded with the Greek coast while raiding it.
salyes.e: Massalia appealed to the Roman Republic, and campaigns in 125 to 123 BCE under Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Sextius Calvinus destroyed Entremont. Their king Teutomalius fled to the Allobroges. In 122 BCE the Romans founded Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence) nearby, and the territory became part of Gallia Narbonensis.

state-of-the-teutonic-order.t: Crusader state of the Teutonic Knights on the Baltic, which conquered the pagan Prussians, ruled from Marienburg and became the Duchy of Prussia in 1525.
state-of-the-teutonic-order.o: In 1226 Duke Konrad of Masovia invited the Teutonic Order to fight the pagan Prussians, and Emperor Frederick II's Golden Bull of Rimini granted Grand Master Hermann von Salza the conquered lands. Over fifty years the knights subdued Prussia, absorbing the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1237 and seizing Danzig in 1308.
state-of-the-teutonic-order.r: The Grand Master ruled from Marienburg from 1309 through a network of brick castles, with commanders governing districts. The knights brought in German peasants and townsmen, founded towns such as Thorn and Königsberg and profited from the grain and amber trade through the Hanseatic League. Under Winrich von Kniprode in the 14th century the state reached its height, launching crusades against Lithuania.
state-of-the-teutonic-order.e: Defeat by Poland and Lithuania at Grunwald in 1410 and the Thirteen Years War cost the Order West Prussia at the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned Lutheran and secularised the rest as the Duchy of Prussia.

sicel-league.t: Short-lived union of the native Sicel towns of eastern Sicily under Ducetius, who tried to resist the Greek cities in the mid-5th century BCE.
sicel-league.o: The Sicels were the native people of eastern Sicily, gradually pushed inland by the Greek colonies. After the fall of the tyrants in Syracuse and Acragas in the 460s BCE, the Sicel leader Ducetius united most Sicel communities, apart from Hybla, around 460 BCE.
sicel-league.r: Ducetius founded new towns, including Menaenum and Palike, beside the sanctuary of the Palici, twin gods worshipped at volcanic pools that served as a place of oaths and refuge for slaves. He took Morgantina and Inessa and attacked Acragan and Syracusan territory. The league was a military federation built around his leadership.
sicel-league.e: In 450 BCE Syracuse and Acragas defeated Ducetius at Nomae; he surrendered and was exiled to Corinth. He returned to found Kale Akte on the north coast but died around 440 BCE, and Syracuse absorbed the Sicel towns. The Sicels were gradually Hellenised.

saka.t: Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the eastern steppe, famed for gold-rich kurgans, who later carved out kingdoms in Bactria, Sistan and north-western India.
saka.o: The Saka were the eastern branch of the wider Scythian world, recorded by Persian inscriptions and Greek writers from about the 7th century BCE. Achaemenid texts name several groups, among them the Saka Tigraxauda, the 'pointed-hat' Saka, and the Saka Haumavarga, and Cyrus the Great and Darius I campaigned against them across the Syr Darya.
saka.r: They were not one state but a loose world of pastoral tribes ruled by chieftains and warrior elites. Mobile herding of horses, sheep and cattle supported them, alongside trade with oasis towns. Their burials, such as the Issyk kurgan with its 'Golden Man' and the frozen tombs of Pazyryk and Berel, display the animal-style art of gold plaques, felt and horse trappings shared across the steppe.
saka.e: In the 2nd century BCE pressure from the Yuezhi drove many Saka south into Bactria, Sistan and the Indus valley, where they founded the Indo-Scythian kingdoms. Others were absorbed by the Wusun and later Turkic peoples. Khotanese and Tumshuqese, the Saka languages of the Tarim Basin, survived into the 10th century.

severians-balkan.t: Slavic tribe in north-eastern Bulgaria whom the Bulgars under Asparuh placed to guard the eastern passes of the Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.o: Known mainly from Byzantine chronicles, the Severi were a Slavic tribe that settled in Moesia in the 7th century, in the area between the Danube delta and the eastern Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.r: They lived as a tribal people under their own chiefs. When the Bulgars arrived under Asparuh in 680–681, Theophanes records that the Severi were moved to guard the passes towards Byzantium, while the Seven Slavic Tribes held other borders.
severians-balkan.e: They became part of the First Bulgarian Empire, keeping their own leaders for some time; in the 760s the Byzantine emperor Constantine V captured Slavun, chief of the Severi. They then merged into the Bulgarian population.

sanjak-of-alexandretta.t: A Syrian district with a large Turkish population whose status, disputed between France and Turkey, ended in its annexation by Turkey.
sanjak-of-alexandretta.o: By the Treaty of Ankara of 1921 France agreed that the district of Alexandretta, which included Antioch and a large Turkish-speaking population alongside Arabs, Alawites and Armenians, should have a special administrative regime within French-ruled Syria. It formed an autonomous sanjak attached first to the State of Aleppo and then to Syria.
sanjak-of-alexandretta.r: Turkish was an official language and the sanjak had its own administration. When France promised Syria independence in 1936, Turkey demanded the district. The League of Nations drafted a statute making it a separate entity, and elections held in 1938 under Turkish military presence gave Turks a majority in the assembly.
sanjak-of-alexandretta.e: In September 1938 the assembly proclaimed Hatay State, which joined Turkey in 1939. Syria has never formally recognised the loss.

socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.t: Tito's communist federation of six South Slav republics, which broke with Stalin, led the Non-Aligned Movement and broke apart in war in the 1990s.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.o: Tito's Partisans emerged victorious from the Second World War after defeating occupiers, the Independent State of Croatia and the Chetniks. The AVNOJ council at Jajce in 1943 had set out a federal state, Democratic Federal Yugoslavia was formed in 1945, and on 29 November 1945 the monarchy was abolished and a federal people's republic proclaimed, with six republics.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.r: After Tito's split with Stalin in 1948, Yugoslavia developed its own socialism based on workers' self-management and market elements, and in 1961 co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade. Its citizens could travel and work abroad. The 1974 constitution decentralised power to the republics and autonomous provinces, while Tito ruled as president for life.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.e: After Tito's death in 1980, debt, inflation and nationalism grew, notably under Slobodan Milošević in Serbia. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, followed by Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, amid war. In April 1992 Serbia and Montenegro formed the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

state-of-syria.t: The unified Syrian state created by France in 1925 from Damascus and Aleppo, the setting of the Great Syrian Revolt.
state-of-syria.o: France merged the State of Damascus and the State of Aleppo into the State of Syria with effect from 1 January 1925, with Damascus as capital and Subhi Barakat as president; the Alawite and Jabal Druze states remained separate.
state-of-syria.r: Months after its creation, the Great Syrian Revolt spread from the Jabal Druze to Damascus and the countryside; French forces shelled Damascus in October 1925 and suppressed the rising by 1927. French high commissioners appointed governments led by Ahmad Nami and later Taj al-Din al-Hasani. A Constituent Assembly elected in 1928, dominated by the nationalist National Bloc under Hashim al-Atassi, drafted a constitution.
state-of-syria.e: In May 1930 the French high commissioner promulgated a modified constitution, turning the state into the Syrian Republic.

shechem.t: Shechem, a fortified Canaanite city in the central hills whose ruler Labayu challenged Egyptian control in the Amarna age.
shechem.o: Shechem, at Tell Balata near modern Nablus, commanded the pass between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. It appears in Egyptian execration texts and in an account of a campaign by Senusret III of the Middle Kingdom of Egypt, and by the 17th century BCE was ringed by massive walls.
shechem.r: Its rulers built a great fortress-temple, among the largest in Canaan, and controlled the highlands around. In the 14th century BCE its king Labayu expanded his territory at the expense of neighbouring vassals of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, provoking complaints in the Amarna letters; his sons carried on the struggle.
shechem.e: The Canaanite city declined in the 12th century BCE. Shechem later became a centre of the Kingdom of Israel and of the Samaritans, and the Bible preserves memories of its temple of El-Berith.

syrian-republic.t: The Syrian state of 1930-1958, which won independence from France and then fell into military coups before uniting with Egypt.
syrian-republic.o: The French high commissioner promulgated a constitution in May 1930 that turned the State of Syria into the Syrian Republic under the French mandate. Muhammad Ali al-Abid became its first president in 1932.
syrian-republic.r: The National Bloc negotiated a 1936 treaty that France never ratified. Shukri al-Quwatli, elected president in 1943, led the country to full independence when the last French troops left on 17 April 1946. Defeat in the 1948 war with Israel discredited the civilian leadership, and in 1949 three coups followed, by Husni al-Za'im, Sami al-Hinnawi and Adib Shishakli, who ruled until 1954. Parliamentary rule then returned, with the Ba'ath party gaining influence.
syrian-republic.e: Fearing communist influence and seeking Arab unity, Syrian leaders asked Egypt for union, and in February 1958 Syria joined the United Arab Republic.

side.t: Side, a Pamphylian port city with its own language and script, famous for its harbour and later its slave market.
side.o: Greeks from Cyme in Aeolis settled Side in the 7th century BCE on a peninsula of the Pamphylian coast. According to legend, they soon forgot Greek and spoke the local language, called Sidetic, written in a unique alphabet. The city's name means pomegranate.
side.r: Side was a self-governing port that thrived on trade and shipbuilding. It surrendered to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 333 BCE and came under the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire. In 190 BCE a Rhodian fleet defeated Hannibal off its shore.
side.e: In the 1st century BCE Side became a centre for Cilician pirates, who sold captives in its market. The Romans suppressed piracy, and in 25 BCE the city was included in the province of Galatia, flourishing under Rome.

smyrna.t: Ancient Greek city on the Gulf of Izmir, a claimed birthplace of Homer, destroyed by Lydia and refounded in the Hellenistic age.
smyrna.o: Old Smyrna, at Bayraklı on the Gulf of Izmir, was settled by Aeolian Greeks c. 1000 BCE and taken over by Ionian exiles from Colophon, probably in the 8th century BCE. It developed into one of the first Greek cities with planned streets and stone walls, and claimed to be the birthplace of Homer.
smyrna.r: The city prospered from the fertile Hermus plain. Its temple of Athena is among the earliest monumental Ionian sanctuaries. It was not one of the original twelve members of the Ionian League. Smyrna fought the Kingdom of Lydia, resisting Gyges, but Alyattes destroyed it c. 600 BCE, after which it survived only as villages.
smyrna.e: Antigonus and Lysimachus refounded Smyrna on the slopes of Mount Pagus c. 300 BCE, and it joined the Ionian League. It sided with Rome against Antiochus III and passed into the province of Asia after 133 BCE, growing into the modern city of Izmir.

swedish-wismar.t: Baltic port in Mecklenburg held by Sweden from the Peace of Westphalia until 1803, when it was pawned to Mecklenburg-Schwerin for a century.
swedish-wismar.o: Sweden occupied Wismar during the Thirty Years' War, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave it the town, the island of Poel and the district of Neukloster as an imperial fief. Wismar became one of Sweden's footholds on the southern Baltic, with Swedish Pomerania and Bremen-Verden.
swedish-wismar.r: Sweden turned Wismar into a heavily fortified naval base and placed there, from 1653, the Wismar Tribunal, the supreme court of appeal for all of Sweden's German possessions. The town kept its Hanseatic council and German law, while a Swedish governor commanded the garrison. Its trade suffered from the wars fought over it, and Danish and Prussian forces besieged it in 1675 and 1711-1716.
swedish-wismar.e: In 1803 Sweden pawned Wismar to the Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin for 1,250,000 riksdaler for 100 years, in the Treaty of Malmö. The loan was never repaid, and in 1903 Sweden renounced its rights, leaving Wismar to Germany.

smyrna-zone.t: The Greek-administered zone around Smyrna after the First World War, which ended in the destruction of the city in 1922.
smyrna-zone.o: With the approval of the Allies, Greek troops landed at Smyrna on 15 May 1919, ostensibly to protect the large Greek Orthodox population. The landing was marred by killings of Turks and helped ignite the Turkish national movement. The Treaty of Sevres of 1920 placed the zone under Greek administration, with a plebiscite on union with Greece after five years.
smyrna-zone.r: The High Commissioner Aristeidis Stergiadis ran the zone and tried, with mixed success, to treat Muslims and Christians equally. A Greek university, the Ionian University, was planned under the mathematician Constantin Caratheodory. The zone served as the base for the Greek army's offensives deep into Anatolia in 1920-1921.
smyrna-zone.e: After the Greek defeat at Dumlupinar in August 1922, Turkish forces entered Smyrna on 9 September. A great fire destroyed the Greek and Armenian quarters, and the Christian population fled. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and population exchange confirmed the city's place in the Republic of Turkey.

sultanate-of-angoche.t: A Swahili Muslim sultanate on the Mozambique coast that traded inland past the Portuguese and resisted colonial conquest until 1910.
sultanate-of-angoche.o: Angoche was founded on coastal islands in the late 15th century by Swahili settlers linked to Kilwa. It was already an established trading town when the Portuguese arrived, and it served as an alternative outlet for gold and ivory from the Zambezi valley, bypassing Portuguese-controlled Sofala and later Mozambique Island.
sultanate-of-angoche.r: The sultan ruled with a council of leading Swahili lineages, and the town was a centre of Islamic learning and Sufi brotherhoods for the coast. Trade in ivory and, in the 19th century, slaves for French and Brazilian buyers made it wealthy. Under Musa Mohamed Sahib Quanto in the 1860s Angoche expanded inland among the Makua.
sultanate-of-angoche.e: Portuguese forces occupied Angoche in 1861 and again in the 1890s, but resistance led by the Makua and Swahili continued. Sultan Farelay fought on until his capture in 1910, when the sultanate was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

scalovians.t: Baltic people of the lower Neman river, between the Prussians and Lithuanians, conquered by the Teutonic Order in the 1270s.
scalovians.o: The Scalovians, or Skalvians, lived on both banks of the lower Neman in what is now the Kaliningrad region of Russia and western Lithuania. They were related to the Prussians and Curonians, and their territory lay on the river route linking the Baltic coast with inland Lithuania.
scalovians.r: They lived in farming and fishing communities defended by hillforts, including Ragnit on the Neman. Their position made them a buffer between the Teutonic Order and Lithuania, and they traded and intermarried with both Prussians and Lithuanians.
scalovians.e: The Teutonic Order campaigned against them from the 1270s, and by 1277 Scalovia was subdued. The Order built Ragnit castle in 1289 on the site of a Scalovian fort. Many Scalovians fled to Lithuania, and the region later became part of the area known as Lithuania Minor.

saguntum.t: The Iberian town of Arse, Rome's ally, whose siege and destruction by Hannibal in 219 BCE started the Second Punic War.
saguntum.o: Saguntum, called Arse by its inhabitants, grew in the 5th century BCE on a long rocky hill above the Palancia river, near the coast north of Valencia, within the Edetanian world. Greek writers wrongly believed it had been founded by settlers from Zakynthos.
saguntum.r: It was a prosperous Iberian town trading by sea with Greeks and Phoenicians and minting silver coins with the legend Arse. In the 220s BCE it made an alliance with Rome, though it lay south of the Ebro, the limit agreed between Rome and Hasdrubal in 226 BCE.
saguntum.e: In 219 BCE Hannibal besieged Saguntum for eight months and took it, and Rome's declaration of war on Carthage followed. The Scipios recaptured the town in 212 BCE and restored its people. Saguntum flourished as a Roman municipium, whose theatre and walls still survive.

swedish-gold-coast.t: Sweden's brief foothold in West Africa, centred on Carolusborg at Cape Coast, lost to Denmark and the Dutch within thirteen years.
swedish-gold-coast.o: The Swedish Africa Company was founded in 1649 by Louis De Geer, a Dutch-born industrialist in Swedish service. Its agent Hendrik Carloff obtained land from the local Fante rulers, and in 1653 the company built Fort Carolusborg at Cape Coast, on the coast of modern Ghana, along with smaller lodges.
swedish-gold-coast.r: The colony was a trading enterprise, exchanging European goods for gold, ivory and enslaved people. It relied on agreements with local African rulers and on Dutch and Swedish crews, and it faced constant rivalry from the Dutch West India Company and the Danes.
swedish-gold-coast.e: In 1658 Carloff, now serving Denmark, seized Carolusborg. The fort changed hands several times before the Dutch took it in 1663, ending Swedish presence in Africa. As Cape Coast Castle under the English from 1664, it became one of the main centres of the British slave trade.

seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Aleppo share of Tutush's realm under his son Ridwan, a weak state that paid tribute to Antioch and allied with the Assassins.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.o: After Tutush I fell in battle in 1095, his son Ridwan secured Aleppo and northern Syria, while his brother Duqaq took Damascus. Their quarrels divided Muslim Syria at the moment the First Crusade arrived.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.r: Ridwan lost territory to the Principality of Antioch and paid tribute to Tancred. Unpopular with the Sunni population, he relied on the Nizari Ismailis, allowing them a mission house in Aleppo and using their assassins against rivals. He also rejected a Seljuk-led counter-crusade in 1111 by closing the city's gates. After his death in 1113 his sons Alp Arslan al-Akhras and Sultan Shah were puppets of the eunuch Lu'lu' and other officers.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Threatened by the Franks, Aleppo's notables turned to outside protectors, and in 1117-1118 the city passed to the Artuqid Ilghazi, later part of the Artuqids of Mardin's sphere and then the Zengid dynasty.

second-taifa-of-mertola.t: A Sufi-led rebel state in the Algarve whose leader Ibn Qasi rose against the Almoravids and opened the way for the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-mertola.o: Ibn Qasi, a former tax official turned Sufi teacher, gathered disciples called the Muridun in the western Algarve. In 1144, as Almoravid rule weakened, his followers seized Mértola, and he proclaimed himself imam and mahdi.
second-taifa-of-mertola.r: The movement combined religious reform with rebellion against Almoravid taxes and jurists. Ibn Qasi was allied for a time with Ibn al-Mundhir of Silves and Sidray ibn Wazir of Beja, but they soon turned against him. He was among the first to appeal to the Almohads in Morocco, then sought support from Afonso I of Portugal.
second-taifa-of-mertola.e: His alliance with Portugal angered his own supporters, who killed him in Silves in 1151. Mértola passed to the Almohads, and his mystical writings were later studied by Ibn Arabi.

seha-river-land.t: The Seha River Land, a Hittite vassal kingdom of western Anatolia, caught between the Hittites and the Mycenaean Greeks.
seha-river-land.o: The Seha River Land formed part of the old Arzawa coalition in the valley of a western Anatolian river, probably the Bakırçay or Gediz. After the fall of Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, Mursili II confirmed Manapa-Tarhunta as its king under a Hittite treaty.
seha-river-land.r: Its rulers governed the river valley and, at times, the nearby island of Lazpa, probably Lesbos. A letter from Manapa-Tarhunta reports on events in Wilusa, and King Masturi married a sister of Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire.
seha-river-land.e: Under Tudhaliya IV a king backed by Ahhiyawa rebelled and was defeated. The kingdom fades from the record with the collapse of the Hittite Empire c. 1180 BCE.

serbian-vojvodina.t: Self-proclaimed Serbian autonomous province in southern Hungary during the revolution of 1848, whose name lives on in today's Vojvodina.
serbian-vojvodina.o: As Hungary asserted its independence in spring 1848, Serbs of southern Hungary feared Magyarisation. A national assembly at Sremski Karlovci in May 1848 proclaimed the Serbian Vojvodina in Srem, Baranya, Bačka and Banat, elected Josif Rajačić patriarch and Colonel Stevan Šupljikac voivode, and set up a Main Board led by Đorđe Stratimirović.
serbian-vojvodina.r: The Vojvodina was a wartime administration rather than a settled state. Its forces, joined by volunteers from the Principality of Serbia, fought Hungarian revolutionary armies in bitter ethnic warfare across Bačka and Banat. The Serb leaders allied with the Habsburg court against Budapest, hoping for autonomy as a reward.
serbian-vojvodina.e: After Hungary's defeat in 1849, Vienna created the Voivodeship of Serbia and Banat of Temeschwar, an Austrian crown land run by German-speaking officials rather than by the Serbs. The name Vojvodina, however, became established for the region.

second-french-empire.t: Napoleon III's empire, which rebuilt Paris, built railways and a colonial empire, and collapsed after defeat by Prussia at Sedan in 1870.
second-french-empire.o: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president of the French Second Republic, seized dictatorial power in a coup in December 1851. A plebiscite approved restoring the empire, and on 2 December 1852 he became Emperor Napoleon III.
second-french-empire.r: The early empire was authoritarian, with censorship and managed elections. Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris with boulevards and sewers, and railways, banks and department stores expanded. France fought in the Crimea, helped unify Italy and gained Nice and Savoy in 1860, but the Mexican intervention failed. From 1860 the regime liberalised, becoming a parliamentary 'Liberal Empire' under Émile Ollivier in 1870.
second-french-empire.e: Provoked by Bismarck, France declared war on Prussia in July 1870. Napoleon III was captured at Sedan on 2 September, and two days later the French Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. He died in exile in England in 1873.

sidicini.t: Small Oscan people of northern Campania whose appeal for help against the Samnites in 343 BCE set off Rome's first war with Samnium.
sidicini.o: The Sidicini lived around Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano) in the hills between the Roccamonfina volcano and the Volturno, bordering the Aurunci and Campanians. They were an Oscan-speaking people, possibly related to the Samnites or the Ausones; their earlier history is unknown.
sidicini.r: Known mainly from Livy, they formed a small community centred on Teanum, which later issued its own coins in Oscan. In 343 BCE the Samnites attacked them; the Sidicini sought help from Capua, and Capua's appeal to Rome began the First Samnite War. They joined the Latins and Campanians against Rome in 340 BCE.
sidicini.e: Rome founded the Latin colony of Cales on land taken from the Sidicini and Aurunci in 334 BCE, ending their independence. Teanum Sidicinum became a Roman ally and later a municipium and colony.

swedish-livonia.t: Livonia under the Swedish crown, home to Riga, then the largest city of the Swedish realm, and to the university founded at Dorpat in 1632.
swedish-livonia.o: Gustav II Adolf captured Riga from Poland-Lithuania in 1621, and the Truce of Altmark in 1629 confirmed Swedish possession of most of the Duchy of Livonia, including southern Estonia and the island of Ösel after 1645. Latgale in the south-east stayed Polish.
swedish-livonia.r: A Swedish governor-general ruled from Riga, while the Baltic German knighthood kept its diet and Lutheran church. Gustav II Adolf founded the University of Dorpat in 1632, and the pastor Ernst Glück translated the Bible into Latvian in 1685-1689. Riga's exports of grain, flax and timber made it the busiest port in the Swedish empire. Charles XI's reduction of noble estates provoked the opposition of Johann Reinhold Patkul.
swedish-livonia.e: In the Great Northern War Russian troops besieged and took Riga in 1710 after a plague-stricken defence. The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 ceded Livonia to Russia, where it became the Governorate of Livonia. Later Latvians and Estonians remembered the Swedish period as 'the good Swedish times'.

strymonians.t: Slavic tribe of the lower Strymon valley that joined the sieges of Thessalonica and long resisted Byzantine control.
strymonians.o: Known mainly from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius and Byzantine chronicles, the Strymonians settled along the lower Strymon (Struma) in the early 7th century and took part in the Slavic attacks on Thessalonica around 615.
strymonians.r: They were a tribal people under local chiefs, farming the river valley and controlling routes between Thessalonica and Constantinople. In the 670s they again joined attacks on Thessalonica, and in 688 Justinian II campaigned against them and moved many Slavs to Anatolia.
strymonians.e: Byzantium gradually brought the lower Strymon under control, creating the theme of Strymon by the 9th century, while the upper valley passed to the First Bulgarian Empire. The tribe merged into the population of both.

shubria.t: Shubria, a Hurrian kingdom of the upper Tigris highlands that sheltered fugitives from Assyria until Esarhaddon conquered it.
shubria.o: Shubria lay in the mountains north of the upper Tigris, between Assyria and the Kingdom of Urartu. It emerged as a kingdom after the Late Bronze Age, inhabited by Hurrian speakers whose culture survived longer there than elsewhere.
shubria.r: Its kings, ruling from Uppumu, played Assyria and Urartu against each other. Shubria was known as a refuge where fugitives, deserters and escaped slaves from the Assyrian Empire could find asylum, a practice its kings defended.
shubria.e: When King Ik-Teshub refused to hand over fugitives, Esarhaddon of the Assyrian Empire captured Uppumu in 673 BCE and annexed Shubria, recording the campaign in a letter to the god Ashur.

swiss-confederation.t: Modern Switzerland, a federal state of cantons that became a model of neutrality, direct democracy and multilingual government.
swiss-confederation.o: Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 replaced the centralised Helvetic Republic with a confederation of 19 cantons, including new cantons such as Vaud, Aargau and Ticino formed from former subject lands. After Napoleon's fall the Federal Treaty of 1815 and the Congress of Vienna added Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel and recognised Swiss neutrality.
swiss-confederation.r: Tensions between liberal Protestant and conservative Catholic cantons led to the Sonderbund War of 1847. The federal constitution of 1848 created a federal state with a two-chamber parliament and a seven-member Federal Council, with Bern as federal city. Referendums and popular initiatives were added in 1874 and 1891. Industry, banking and tourism grew, and German, French, Italian and Romansh are national languages.
swiss-confederation.e: Switzerland stayed neutral in both world wars. Women gained the federal vote only in 1971, and the canton of Jura was created in 1979. It joined the United Nations in 2002 but remains outside the European Union.

samnite-league.t: Confederation of the Oscan-speaking peoples of the southern Apennines, Rome's toughest opponent in Italy during three Samnite Wars.
samnite-league.o: The Samnites lived in the mountains of modern Molise and inland Campania. They believed they descended from Sabines who had migrated south in a 'sacred spring'. By the 5th century BCE they had formed a confederation of four peoples, the Pentri, Caraceni, Caudini and Hirpini, with Bovianum as a main centre.
samnite-league.r: Each people (touto) was governed by an elected magistrate, the meddix tuticus, and the league acted together in war. Society was rural, living in villages and hill forts. The great sanctuary at Pietrabbondante, with its temple and theatre, was a federal centre. Samnite warriors were famed for their armour, and their expansion carried Oscan speech into Campania, Lucania and Bruttium.
samnite-league.e: Rome fought three Samnite Wars from 343 to 290 BCE. The Samnites trapped a Roman army at the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE but lost at Sentinum in 295 BCE and accepted Roman alliance in 290 BCE. They later backed Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and Sulla crushed them at the Colline Gate in 82 BCE.

sambians.t: Prussian people of the Sambian peninsula, the world's richest source of Baltic amber, whose conquest in 1255 led to the founding of Königsberg.
sambians.o: The Sambians lived on the Sambian peninsula between the Vistula and Curonian lagoons, in today's Kaliningrad region. Their amber had reached the Roman world, and in the Viking Age Scandinavian traders settled at Wiskiauten nearby. Adam of Bremen in the 11th century described the Sambians as humane people with much fur.
sambians.r: Sambia was the most populous and wealthy Prussian land, with nobles holding fortified seats and a strong warrior class. Amber, furs and slaves were traded across the Baltic. The Sambians kept the Prussian pagan religion and resisted Danish and Polish missions.
sambians.e: In 1255 a crusade led by King Ottokar II of Bohemia subdued Sambia, and the Teutonic Order founded Königsberg, named in his honour. The Sambians rose again from 1260 under Glande but were defeated. Many nobles joined the Order's service, and their land became Order territory and the Bishopric of Samland.

senones.t: Gallic people of the Yonne around Sens, a branch of whom sacked Rome in about 390 BCE and settled on the Adriatic coast.
senones.o: The Senones held the land along the Yonne and the upper Seine, with Agedincum (Sens) as their chief town. Livy and Polybius record that part of the people crossed the Alps around 400 BCE; led by Brennus, they defeated the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome, then settled on the Adriatic coast around Sena Gallica (Senigallia).
senones.r: In Gaul they were a powerful people with a council of nobles. Caesar made Cavarinus their king, but the Senones drove him out in 54 BCE, a sign of resistance to Roman-backed kingship.
senones.e: The Italian Senones were defeated by Rome in 283 BCE. In Gaul Caesar had the rebel leader Acco flogged to death in 53 BCE, and the Senones joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Agedincum became Sens, later the seat of a powerful archbishop.

swedish-ingria.t: Swedish province at the head of the Gulf of Finland that cut Russia off from the Baltic, until Peter the Great built St Petersburg on its land.
swedish-ingria.o: Sweden captured the fortresses of Ivangorod, Jama and Koporye during the Livonian War, confirmed by the Truce of Plussa in 1583, but returned them to Russia in 1595. During the Time of Troubles Sweden reconquered the area, and the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617 gave Ingria to Sweden permanently, cutting Russia off from the sea.
swedish-ingria.r: Ingria was a thinly populated frontier, governed from Narva together with Estonia. Many Orthodox inhabitants left, and Lutheran Finns from Savonia and Karelia settled, forming the Ingrian Finns. The fortress of Nyenskans and the town of Nyen at the mouth of the Neva controlled trade with Russia.
swedish-ingria.e: In the Great Northern War Peter the Great captured Nyenskans in 1703 and founded St Petersburg nearby. Narva fell in 1704, and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 confirmed Ingria as Russian. It became the core of the St Petersburg Governorate.
swedish-ingria.la: Finnish, Swedish, Russian, Votic and Izhorian

serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.t: Leftist republic proclaimed in Pécs in 1921 as Yugoslav troops prepared to hand the region back to Horthy's Hungary.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.o: Yugoslav forces occupied Pécs and the coal-mining region of Baranya in November 1918. The area became a refuge for Hungarian socialists, communists and liberals fleeing the White Terror. When the Treaty of Trianon returned the area to Hungary, they proclaimed the Serbian-Hungarian Baranya-Baja Republic on 14 August 1921, with the painter Petar Dobrović as president.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.r: The republic was a last-minute attempt to stop the return of Horthy's regime, and hoped either for independence or union with Yugoslavia. It had a provisional government and relied on miners' support, but had no means of defence once Yugoslav troops left.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.e: Hungarian troops entered Pécs on 21 and 22 August 1921, ending the republic after about a week. Thousands of its supporters fled to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and the region returned to the Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946).

sican.t: A theocratic culture of Peru's north coast, centred on the pyramids of Batán Grande, that dominated Andean goldworking and trade in arsenical bronze.
sican.o: The Sicán culture, also called Lambayeque, emerged around 750 in the La Leche and Lambayeque valleys, in the former territory of the Moche. A legend recorded by the Spanish tells of Naymlap, who arrived by sea with a fleet of balsa rafts and founded a dynasty there.
sican.r: Middle Sicán, about 900 to 1100, was ruled from the Sicán Precinct at Batán Grande, with large adobe pyramids such as Huaca Loro. Elite tombs contained tonnes of grave goods, including gold masks and arsenical copper. Sicán produced arsenical bronze on a large scale and used naipes, small copper axe-shaped objects, possibly as a form of currency. Trade reached Ecuador for spondylus shell. Its art centred on the Sicán Lord, a figure with winged eyes.
sican.e: Around 1100 a severe drought followed by El Niño floods led to the burning and abandonment of Batán Grande. Late Sicán continued at Túcume until the region was conquered by the Kingdom of Chimor around 1375.

sulayhid-dynasty.t: An Isma'ili dynasty that united Yemen under the Fatimid banner and is remembered for Queen Arwa, one of the few women to rule in medieval Islam.
sulayhid-dynasty.o: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi, a judge's son and Isma'ili missionary for the Fatimid Caliphate, rose in revolt in the Haraz mountains in 1047. Within two decades he had taken Sanaa, Zabid and Aden and brought most of Yemen under his rule, recognising the Fatimid caliph in Cairo.
sulayhid-dynasty.r: The Sulayhids spread the Fatimid mission to Oman and western India. After Ali was killed by the Najahid dynasty, power passed to his son al-Mukarram Ahmad and then to Ahmad's wife, Arwa bint Ahmad, who governed from Dhu Jibla for some fifty years, built its great mosque and was given authority over the Fatimid mission in Yemen. Governors such as the Zurayids ruled Aden for them.
sulayhid-dynasty.e: When the Fatimids split over succession in 1130, Arwa backed the infant al-Tayyib, founding the Tayyibi branch of Isma'ilism. After her death in 1138 the state broke apart among the Zurayid dynasty, the Hamdanid sultanate of Yemen and others. Tayyibi leadership later moved to India, where the Bohras continue it.

state-of-aleppo.t: The French-created state of northern Syria around Aleppo, which existed for four years before being merged into the State of Syria.
state-of-aleppo.o: Following the defeat of the Arab Kingdom of Syria, the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud created the State of Aleppo in September 1920. It covered northern Syria and the Euphrates valley and included the Sanjak of Alexandretta, which had a special regime.
state-of-aleppo.r: The state was governed by local notables under French supervision; its first governor was Kamil Pasha al-Qudsi. Aleppo's merchants suffered from the new borders, which cut the city off from its Anatolian hinterland after the 1921 Treaty of Ankara with Turkey. In 1922 the state joined the Syrian Federation.
state-of-aleppo.e: At the end of 1924 France merged the states of Aleppo and Damascus into the State of Syria, effective January 1925, while Alexandretta kept its autonomy.

sophene.t: Sophene, an Armenian kingdom in the upper Euphrates valley, ruled by a branch of the Orontid dynasty until Tigranes the Great absorbed it.
sophene.o: Sophene lay west of the Tigris sources around modern Elazığ, the old land of Isuwa. In the 3rd century BCE an Orontid prince, Arsames, ruled it and founded Arsamosata. It was part of the wider Armenian world of the Kingdom of Armenia (Orontid), though often under Seleucid overlordship.
sophene.r: Its kings controlled important crossings of the Euphrates and Tigris and the routes between Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Antiochus III appointed Zariadres as governor; after Rome defeated Antiochus in 189 BCE, Zariadres declared himself king. The court mixed Iranian and Greek traditions.
sophene.e: Around 95 BCE Tigranes the Great of the Kingdom of Armenia (Artaxiad) deposed its last king, Artanes, and annexed Sophene, uniting Armenia.

sidon.t: Sidon, one of the oldest Phoenician cities, whose kings led the Persian navy and whose name long stood for all Phoenicians.
sidon.o: Sidon stood on a promontory with offshore islets forming a harbour on the southern Lebanese coast. Inhabited since prehistory, it was a Canaanite port in the Amarna age, and in Homer and the Bible Sidonians means Phoenicians in general, a sign of its early prestige.
sidon.r: Its kings ruled a merchant city famous for glass and purple cloth, and honoured the healing god Eshmun at a great sanctuary outside the city. Under the Achaemenid Empire Sidon was the leading Phoenician city and supplied the core of the Persian fleet; the inscribed sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II survives.
sidon.e: Esarhaddon of the Assyrian Empire razed the city in 677 BCE, and Artaxerxes III burned it again after King Tennes rebelled. In 332 BCE Sidon opened its gates to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire, who installed Abdalonymus as king, ending its independent history.

scordisci.t: Celtic people at the meeting of the Sava and Danube who founded Singidunum, modern Belgrade, and harried Roman Macedonia for two centuries.
scordisci.o: After the Celtic invasion of Greece under Brennus failed in 279 BCE, survivors settled at the confluence of the Sava and Danube. There they merged with local Illyrian and Thracian peoples and formed the Scordisci, with strongholds at Singidunum (Belgrade) and Taurunum (Zemun).
scordisci.r: A warrior aristocracy ruled over a mixed population, dominating the middle Danube from fortified oppida. They minted coins, traded along the river and raided south. In 114 BCE they destroyed a Roman army under Gaius Porcius Cato in Macedonia, and wars with Rome followed for decades. The Dacian king Burebista defeated them in the mid-1st century BCE.
scordisci.e: Tiberius subdued the Scordisci during his Pannonian campaigns of 12–9 BCE, and they became allies of Rome. By the early 1st century CE they were absorbed into the provinces of Pannonia and Moesia, and the name Singidunum survived as a Roman legionary base.

syrian-federation.t: A short-lived federation of the French-created Syrian states, a step towards reuniting Syria under the mandate.
syrian-federation.o: In June 1922 the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud united the State of Damascus, the State of Aleppo and the Alawite State in a federation, a partial response to nationalist demands for unity.
syrian-federation.r: A federal council of delegates from the three states, under the presidency of Subhi Barakat, handled common affairs, while each state kept its own government and French officials held real power. The capital alternated between Aleppo and Damascus. The federation had a single budget, customs and currency, but nationalists criticised it as a French device that kept Lebanon, the Jabal Druze and Alexandretta apart from Syria. The Alawite State withdrew at the start of 1925.
syrian-federation.e: At the end of 1924 France dissolved the federation, merging Damascus and Aleppo into the State of Syria from January 1925.

second-taifa-of-niebla.t: Niebla's brief independence under Yusuf al-Bitruji during the 1140s revolts against the Almoravids in the far west of al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-niebla.o: In 1145 Yusuf ibn Ahmad al-Bitruji, a local leader, took control of the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, as the revolt begun by Ibn Qasi in the Algarve spread through the south-west.
second-taifa-of-niebla.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Niebla was one of several small regimes that rose and fell in quick succession. Its ruler was drawn into conflicts with Almoravid loyalists in Seville and with neighbouring rebels.
second-taifa-of-niebla.e: Niebla submitted to the Almohads around 1150. A century later it became independent again as the Third Taifa of Niebla.

sugambri.t: A warlike Germanic people of the lower Rhine who repeatedly defied Rome until Augustus deported much of the tribe across the river into Gaul.
sugambri.o: The Sugambri lived on the east bank of the Rhine between the Sieg and the Lippe. They first appear in 55 BCE, when they sheltered survivors of the Usipetes and Tencteri; Julius Caesar bridged the Rhine and ravaged their land in retaliation.
sugambri.r: Little is known of their internal organisation beyond war-leaders and a reputation for raiding. In 16 BCE they crossed the Rhine with the Usipetes and Tencteri and defeated the Roman legate Marcus Lollius, capturing the eagle of the Fifth Legion, an event known as the clades Lolliana. This defeat helped prompt Augustus' German campaigns.
sugambri.e: Drusus attacked them from 12 BCE, and in 8 BCE Tiberius forcibly resettled tens of thousands on the left bank of the Rhine, where they became the Cugerni. Those who stayed merged into later groups, and the name was later absorbed into the Frankish confederation; Frankish kings were poetically called Sicambri.

siphnos.t: Cycladic island that grew briefly rich on gold and silver mines and built a celebrated treasury at Delphi.
siphnos.o: Siphnos, in the western Cyclades, was settled by Ionian Greeks from Athens in the early Iron Age. Its silver and gold deposits, worked since the Bronze Age, made it in the 6th century BCE the richest island of the Aegean, according to Herodotus.
siphnos.r: Siphnians shared their mining income as citizens and gave a tithe to Delphi, where they built the Siphnian Treasury c. 525 BCE, with its famous sculpted frieze. Exiles from Samos extorted a hundred talents from the island c. 524 BCE. Siphnos later sent a ship to Salamis and paid tribute in the Delian League.
siphnos.e: The mines failed, flooded by the sea, which legend blamed on the Siphnians cheating Apollo of his tithe. The island remained a modest community known for its pottery under Hellenistic powers and Rome, losing independence by 146 BCE.

silvanectes.t: Small Gallic people of the forests north of Paris whose town Augustomagus became Senlis.
silvanectes.o: The Silvanectes are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the Suessiones during the conquest. Pliny and Ptolemy record them as a separate people between the Parisii, Bellovaci and Suessiones.
silvanectes.r: Their name has been linked to the forests of the Oise, but nothing is recorded of their society.
silvanectes.e: Under Rome they formed a civitas with Augustomagus (Senlis) as its chief town. It became a bishopric and in 987 the assembly at Senlis elected Hugh Capet king, founding the Kingdom of France.

serbia-and-montenegro.t: Loose union of Serbia and Montenegro that replaced the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and ended when Montenegro voted for independence.
serbia-and-montenegro.o: By 2001 Montenegro's government sought independence from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. To avoid a sudden break, the European Union, through Javier Solana, brokered the Belgrade Agreement of 2002. A Constitutional Charter adopted on 4 February 2003 turned the federation into the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, with Belgrade as its seat.
serbia-and-montenegro.r: The union had a single-chamber parliament, a president, Svetozar Marović, and a small council of ministers handling foreign affairs, defence and human rights. Otherwise the two republics ran their own affairs: Montenegro used the euro and Serbia the dinar, with separate customs systems. The charter allowed either member to hold an independence referendum after three years.
serbia-and-montenegro.e: In a referendum on 21 May 2006, 55.5 percent of Montenegrin voters chose independence, just above the 55 percent threshold set by the EU. Montenegro declared independence on 3 June 2006, and Serbia became the union's legal successor.

sestos.t: Greek city on the European shore of the Hellespont, key to the grain route, whose capture by Athens in 478 BCE closes Herodotus's Histories.
sestos.o: Sestos was founded by Aeolian settlers from Lesbos on the Thracian Chersonese, at the narrows of the Hellespont opposite Abydos. Its harbour and position made it the main crossing point from Asia into Europe.
sestos.r: Sestos lay near the site of Xerxes's bridges in 480 BCE. In 479 to 478 BCE the Athenians under Xanthippus besieged and took it, the episode that ends Herodotus's Histories. It became a key Athenian base for protecting the Black Sea grain route and paid tribute in the Delian League. Greek legend made it the home of Hero, beloved of Leander.
sestos.e: After the Athenian defeat at nearby Aegospotami in 405 BCE, Sestos passed to Sparta, then back to Athens and later to Macedonian and Hellenistic rulers. It came under Roman control by 146 BCE.

saaremaa.t: Estonia's largest island and its seafaring people, the Oeselians, feared raiders of the Baltic who held out against the crusaders until 1227.
saaremaa.o: Saaremaa, known to Germans and Scandinavians as Ösel, was densely settled in the Iron Age, with strong hillforts such as Valjala and Kaarma. Its inhabitants, the Oeselians, appear in Norse sagas and in Henry of Livonia's chronicle as skilled sailors and pirates.
saaremaa.r: Each parish was led by elders, who joined together for raids and defence. The Oeselians attacked the coasts of Denmark and Sweden and, in 1220, destroyed a Swedish garrison at Lihula on the mainland. They also traded across the Baltic and worshipped a god Henry calls Tharapita.
saaremaa.e: In early 1227 a crusader army crossed the frozen sea and took Valjala, forcing the islanders to accept baptism. The island was divided between the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek and the Livonian Order. Its people rebelled repeatedly, notably in 1343, and Saaremaa later passed to Danish Ösel.

sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.t: The transitional Dutch state of 1813–1815, created as Napoleon's empire collapsed, under the returning Prince of Orange as sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.o: After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, French authority in the Netherlands collapsed in November 1813. A provisional government led by Gijsbert Karel van Hogendorp invited William Frederick, son of the last stadtholder, to return. He landed at Scheveningen on 30 November and accepted the title of sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.r: William ruled under a new constitution adopted in 1814, which gave the sovereign wide powers while keeping a States General. The new state rejected the old federal republic in favour of the unitary government created in the Batavian period. Its priority was rebuilding finances and securing allied backing at the Congress of Vienna.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.e: The great powers decided to unite the northern and southern Netherlands as a barrier to France. In March 1815, during Napoleon's Hundred Days, William proclaimed himself king, creating the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

shah-armens.t: A Turkish dynasty that ruled Ahlat on Lake Van for a century, taking the title Shah-Armen, King of the Armenians.
shah-armens.o: In 1100 Sokmen al-Qutbi, a mamluk officer of the Seljuks, took Ahlat on the north-western shore of Lake Van from the Marwanids. His descendants built a principality around the lake that took its title, Shah-Armen, from the region's Armenian past.
shah-armens.r: Ahlat became a thriving city on the trade road between Iran, the Jazira and Anatolia, with a Muslim population alongside many Armenians. The longest reign was that of Sokmen II (1128-1185), who fought the Georgians and married into the Artuqid and Zengid families. The great Seljuk-era cemetery of Ahlat, with its tall carved tombstones, reflects the city's wealth in this period.
shah-armens.e: After Sokmen II died without an heir in 1185, his mamluk Begtimur ruled, followed by other slave commanders amid Ayyubid and Georgian pressure. In 1207 the Ayyubid al-Awhad took Ahlat, ending the dynasty.

sarir.t: A Christian mountain kingdom of the Avars in Dagestan, famed among Arab geographers for its golden throne and its power over the North Caucasus highlands.
sarir.o: Sarir took shape in the 6th century in the Avar lands of mountainous Dagestan, centred on Khunzakh. Arab writers say its name came from a golden throne said to have been given by a Sasanian king. Little is known of its early history beyond these later accounts.
sarir.r: Its kings ruled clans of mountain farmers and herders and were reported to control many thousands of villages. Ibn Rusta and al-Masudi describe a Christian ruler and church while most subjects followed older beliefs. Sarir was tributary to the Khazar Khaganate, allied with the Kingdom of Alania through royal marriages, and fought the Muslim rulers of Derbent.
sarir.e: After the fall of the Khazars, Islam spread into the mountains and the Christian monarchy faded in the 11th and 12th centuries. Its lands and traditions passed to the Avar Khanate, centred on the same town of Khunzakh.
